claim: Visually guided perceptual decisions involve the sequential activation of a hierarchy of cortical areas.
source: Visually guided perceptual decisions involve the sequential activation of a hierarchy of cortical areas.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific understanding about visual processing hierarchies.

claim: It has been hypothesized that a brief time window of activity in each cortical area is sufficient to enable perceptual decisions.
source: It has been hypothesized that a brief time window of activity in each area is sufficient to enable the decision but direct measurements of this time window are lacking.
evidence: The claim references a hypothesis from prior work (Fabre-Thorpe et al., 1998) mentioned later in the text.

claim: Direct measurements of the minimal time window of cortical activity for perceptual decisions are lacking.
source: It has been hypothesized that a brief time window of activity in each area is sufficient to enable the decision but direct measurements of this time window are lacking.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in the literature that the current study addresses.

claim: The threshold duration of activity in visual cortex enabling perceptual discrimination is between 40 and 80 milliseconds.
source: We show that threshold duration of activity in visual cortex enabling perceptual discrimination is between 40 and 80 milliseconds.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by optogenetic silencing experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: During the 40-80 ms time window, the vast majority of neurons discriminating the stimulus fire one or no spikes.
source: During this time window the vast majority of neurons discriminating the stimulus fire one or no spikes and less than 16% fire more than two.
evidence: This finding is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 6.

claim: Less than 16% of discriminating neurons fire more than two spikes during the 40-80 ms time window.
source: During this time window the vast majority of neurons discriminating the stimulus fire one or no spikes and less than 16% fire more than two.
evidence: This is quantified from the electrophysiological data in Figure 6E.

claim: The firing of the first visually evoked spikes in visual cortex is sufficient to enable a perceptual decision.
source: This result establishes that the firing of the first visually evoked spikes in visual cortex is sufficient to enable a perceptual decision.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the combination of optogenetic silencing and electrophysiology data.

claim: A brief time window of activity in each cortical area may be sufficient to enable perceptual decisions based on the number of areas involved in sensory processing.
source: Based on the number of areas likely involved in the processing of sensory stimuli it has been hypothesized that in each area a relatively brief time window of activity may be sufficient to enable a perceptual decision (Fabre-Thorpe et al., 1998).
evidence: This hypothesis is cited from prior work by Fabre-Thorpe et al., 1998.

claim: The minimal time window of activity has never been directly measured for any specific cortical area.
source: Yet, this time window has never been directly measured for any specific area.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that motivates the current study.

claim: Determining the lower temporal limits of cortical activity reveals the minimal output of individual neurons in enabling perceptual decisions.
source: By determining these lower limits and analyzing neuronal activity over this time window within a given area we can establish the minimal output of individual neurons in enabling perceptual decisions and reveal how the stimulus is represented within this time frame in that area.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the experimental approach described.

claim: The minimal time window defines the time that an area must be active for downstream areas to extract sufficient information to enable a perceptual decision.
source: Furthermore, this time window defines the time that an area has to be active such that downstream areas can extract sufficient information to enable a perceptual decision.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional significance of the measured time window.

claim: The relationship between the time window for cortical activity and the time window for an outside observer to extract sufficient information is unclear.
source: How this time window relates to the time window for an outside observer to extract sufficient information (Celebrini et al., 1993; Mazurek and Shadlen, 2002; Shadlen and Newsome, 1998) is not clear.
evidence: This identifies an open question in the field with citations to relevant prior work.

claim: Technical limitations have prevented answers to questions about minimal cortical activity duration.
source: The lack of answers to these questions is largely due to technical limitations.
evidence: This explains why the field has not previously addressed these questions.

claim: It is necessary to demonstrate that a visual area is required for a sensory discrimination task.
source: One key issue is to demonstrate that the visual area of interest is necessary for the sensory discrimination task at hand.
evidence: This is a methodological requirement for interpreting the results.

claim: Activity in a cortical area may carry relevant stimulus information without that area being required for the perceptual decision.
source: Even though activity in a given area may carry relevant stimulus information, that area may not be required for the perceptual decision.
evidence: This is a conceptual point about the distinction between correlation and causation.

claim: Precisely controlling the duration of sensory evoked response in a visual area is a technical challenge.
source: A second challenge is to precisely control the duration of the sensory evoked response of that visual area.
evidence: This identifies a key technical challenge addressed by the current study.

claim: The duration of visually evoked activity in the brain cannot be precisely controlled by the duration of the sensory stimulus.
source: Answering this question has been technically difficult since the duration of visually evoked activity in the brain cannot be precisely controlled by the duration of the sensory stimulus.
evidence: This is a known limitation in the field supported by the citation to Rolls et al., 1999.

claim: A stimulus as brief as 16 ms triggers a response that lasts hundreds of milliseconds in visual cortex.
source: Even a stimulus as brief as 16 ms triggers a response that lasts hundreds of milliseconds in visual cortex (Rolls et al., 1999).
evidence: This is cited from Rolls et al., 1999.

claim: Visual masking has been used to perturb the long lasting neuronal response to a visual stimulus.
source: Presentation of a visual mask at various delays following the stimulus has been used to perturb the long lasting neuronal response to a visual stimulus (Kovács et al., 1995; Lamme et al., 2002; Macknik and Livingstone, 1998; Rolls et al., 1994) and study the effects on perception.
evidence: This describes a prior experimental approach with citations.

claim: It is difficult to disambiguate whether the impact of visual masking on perception is due to suppression of the neuronal response to the stimulus or generation of neuronal activity by the mask.
source: However, whether the impact on perception is due to the suppression of the neuronal response to the stimulus or to the generation of the neuronal activity by the mask (Macknik and Livingstone, 1998) is difficult to disambiguate.
evidence: This identifies a limitation of the visual masking approach with citation.

claim: Visual masks are not area specific but involve the entire visual system.
source: Further, visual masks are not area specific but involve the entire visual system and thus cannot address the minimal duration of activity of a specific visual area.
evidence: This is a limitation of the visual masking approach.

claim: Optogenetic approaches in mice make it possible to selectively, rapidly and completely silence neuronal activity of a given brain area.
source: In the mouse, optogenetic approaches make it possible to selectively, rapidly and completely silence neuronal activity of a given brain area (Lien and Scanziani, 2013; Olsen et al., 2012) at any arbitrary delay after stimulus presentation (Reinhold et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the optogenetic method with citations to prior work.

claim: Optogenetic silencing can be performed at any arbitrary delay after stimulus presentation.
source: In the mouse, optogenetic approaches make it possible to selectively, rapidly and completely silence neuronal activity of a given brain area (Lien and Scanziani, 2013; Olsen et al., 2012) at any arbitrary delay after stimulus presentation (Reinhold et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from Reinhold et al., 2015.

claim: Optogenetic silencing prevents activity from exiting the silenced area rather than adding activity.
source: With optogenetic silencing we do not add activity but instead prevent activity from exiting the silenced area.
evidence: This explains the advantage of optogenetic silencing over visual masking.

claim: Optogenetic silencing allows precise control of the duration of visually evoked activity in a cortical area during a discrimination task.
source: With this approach we can precisely control the duration of visually evoked activity in a cortical area during a discrimination task.
evidence: This describes the key advantage of the optogenetic approach used in the study.

claim: A simple visual discrimination task in mice was developed that depends on visual cortex.
source: Here we developed a simple visual discrimination task in mice that depends on visual cortex.
evidence: This is a primary methodological contribution supported by data in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Primary visual cortex is required only during the initial 80 ms from the onset of stimulus evoked response for a reliable decision to be made.
source: By completely and rapidly silencing primary visual cortex at well-defined intervals after the stimulus appeared in the task, we demonstrate that this cortical area is required only during the initial 80 ms from the onset of stimulus evoked response for a reliable decision to be made.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by optogenetic silencing data in Figure 4.

claim: During the initial 80 ms period, most neurons in primary visual cortex fire one or no action potentials.
source: Importantly, during this period, most neurons in primary visual cortex fire one or no action potentials.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings in Figure 6.

claim: The first action potentials fired by individual neurons play a key role in the execution of the visual discrimination task.
source: Thus, we establish the minimal time window of activity in primary visual cortex sufficient to enable a perceptual discrimination and provide direct evidence for a key role of the first action potentials fired by individual neurons in the execution of the task.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the combination of optogenetic and electrophysiology data.

claim: Mice were head-fixed yet free to run on a treadmill during the visual discrimination task.
source: We developed a visual discrimination task in which mice are head-fixed yet free to run on a treadmill (Figure 1A and Video 1)
evidence: This describes the behavioral setup shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Visual stimuli were circular patches of gratings oriented at different angles.
source: Visual stimuli (circular patches of gratings,~30 degrees, oriented at different angles) shown on a monitor placed on the right side of the animal moved horizontally from the anterior to the posterior end of the monitor at a speed that was proportional to the running speed of the animal.
evidence: This describes the visual stimuli used in the task.

claim: The target stimulus was a grating oriented at 90 degrees.
source: One of the stimuli (a grating oriented at 90 degrees) was the target stimulus, while the other stimulus (a grating oriented at 45 degrees) was the distractor.
evidence: This defines the target stimulus in the discrimination task.

claim: The distractor stimulus was a grating oriented at 45 degrees.
source: One of the stimuli (a grating oriented at 90 degrees) was the target stimulus, while the other stimulus (a grating oriented at 45 degrees) was the distractor.
evidence: This defines the distractor stimulus in the discrimination task.

claim: Mice were rewarded with water for bringing the target stimulus to the center of the monitor and holding it there for a minimum time.
source: Mice were rewarded with water for bringing the target stimulus to the center of the monitor, the reward zone, and holding it there for a minimum time set by the experimenter (~1 s; a trial in which the stimulus is held in the reward zone for at least the minimum time is called a 'stop trial'; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the reward contingency in the task.

claim: The spatial phase of the grating was varied randomly to ensure mice did not solve the task by using local differences in contrast.
source: To ensure that mice did not solve the task by using local differences in contrast between the two gratings, we varied the position of the stripes in the circular patch, i.e. the spatial phase of the grating, randomly.
evidence: This describes a control to ensure the task requires orientation discrimination.

claim: At the beginning of each trial the stimulus was frozen for 350 ms to ensure reproducibility of stimulus position across trials.
source: At the beginning of each trial the stimulus appeared at the anterior end of the monitor and was frozen (i.e. insensitive to the rotation of the treadmill) for 350 ms, after which time the stimulus could be moved by the locomotion of the mouse. This ensured reproducibility of stimulus position across trials in the initial 350 ms.
evidence: This describes a feature of the task design to control stimulus position.

claim: The position of the eye varied little trial to trial during the initial 350 ms of stimulus presentation.
source: Further, during the task the position of the eye varied little trial to trial during the initial 350 ms (the standard deviation of the position of the right eye over this interval across trials was 2.4 ± 0.6 degrees; mean ±std across five mice; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by eye tracking data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Wild type mice learned to perform the task with accuracy above 85% correct in 23 ± 7 days.
source: Mice learned to perform the task with accuracy above 85% correct in 23 ± 7 days (mean ±std; n = 15 wild type mice; Figure 1—figure supplement 2; accuracy is defined as the average of the percentage of stop trials upon target presentation and the percentage of non-stop trials upon distractor presentation; chance level is 50%) completing on average 200 ± 30 trials each day
evidence: This is supported by training data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Transgenic VGat-ChR2-EYFP mice learned the task in 50 ± 20 days.
source: (transgenic mice, VGat-ChR2-EYFP, learned the task in 50 ± 20 days, n = 8 mice; difference in learning rates was significant: p=0.0096, Wilcoxon ranksum test, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by training data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The difference in learning rates between wild type and transgenic mice was significant.
source: (transgenic mice, VGat-ChR2-EYFP, learned the task in 50 ± 20 days, n = 8 mice; difference in learning rates was significant: p=0.0096, Wilcoxon ranksum test, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of learning rates.

claim: Optogenetic silencing of contralateral V1 severely disrupted behavioral performance.
source: During silencing trials, the behavioral performance of mice was severely disrupted (51 ± 3% accuracy; n = 3 mice; Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data during optogenetic silencing shown in Figure 1D.

claim: During cortical silencing trials, mice either kept running regardless of stimulus identity or slowed down indiscriminately for both stimuli.
source: On these trials, mice either kept on running no matter whether the target or distractor was presented (e.g. Figure 1D) or, on a fraction of trials, they sufficiently slowed down to center the grating (i.e. stop trial) but did so indiscriminately for both stimuli (p>0.16, Wilcoxon rank sum test on choice data; e.g. Figure 1D).
evidence: This describes the behavioral patterns observed during cortical silencing.

claim: The discrimination accuracy of an ideal observer during cortical silencing was 55 ± 6%, very close to the actual performance.
source: The discrimination accuracy of the ideal observer was 55 ± 6% (mean ±std, n = 3 mice), hence very close to the actual performance of the task. (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is based on ROC analysis of the behavioral data.

claim: Silencing ipsilateral visual cortex resulted in no substantial impairment in behavioral performance.
source: To exclude the possibility that the optogenetic silencing simply distracted the mice from performing the task, we silenced the right visual cortex (i.e. ipsilateral to the visual stimulus) (Figure 1E). This manipulation resulted in no substantial impairment in the behavioral performance (88 ± 6% accuracy for LED trials versus 89 ± 6% for no LED trials; Figure 1E)
evidence: This control experiment is shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The impairment from optogenetic silencing was specific to the visual cortex processing visual information in the contralateral hemifield.
source: This manipulation resulted in no substantial impairment in the behavioral performance (88 ± 6% accuracy for LED trials versus 89 ± 6% for no LED trials; Figure 1E), thus showing that the impairment was specific to the visual cortex processing visual information in the contralateral hemifield.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the comparison of contralateral and ipsilateral silencing.

claim: Silencing contralateral V1 did not affect the ability of mice to express the decision in a detection task.
source: We verified that silencing visual cortex did not affect the ability of mice to express the decision, that is, to place the stimulus at the center of the monitor. Mice were trained as above but with the target stimulus only. In other words, mice where trained to perform a simple detection rather than a discrimination task. The distance that mice had to run to start the next trial was randomly varied. On trials where the contralateral V1 was silenced, mice centered the target image almost as frequently as in control trials (Figure 1F) demonstrating that contralateral V1 is not required to express the decision.
evidence: This control experiment is shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Lesioned animals performed at chance after surgical removal of contralateral visual cortex.
source: Lesioned animals performed at chance (p>0.3, Wilcoxon rank sum test on choice data, n = 4 mice, Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data after lesions shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The behavioral impairment after lesions was not due to the ten day interval from the last behavioral session.
source: The impairment in behavioral performance was not due to the ten day interval from the last behavioral session because trained control animals experiencing even longer intervals between behavioral sessions remained proficient (accuracy of 80 ± 10%, Figure 2C).
evidence: This control is shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The behavioral impairment after lesions was not due to anesthesia or unspecific impact of surgery.
source: Furthermore the behavioral impairment was not due to either anesthesia or to some unspecific impact of surgery because proficiency was preserved after removing the ipsilateral VC (accuracy of 85%, n = 1 mouse, Figure 2B) or following anesthesia to perform craniotomy for physiological recordings (80 ± 10%, see results below).
evidence: This is supported by control experiments shown in Figure 2B and mentioned in the text.

claim: The visual discrimination task requires visual cortex.
source: Taken together, these results show that this visual discrimination task requires visual cortex.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from both optogenetic silencing and lesion experiments.

claim: The cortical response to the visual stimulus began 40 ± 5 ms after stimulus onset.
source: The cortical response to the visual stimulus began 40 ± 5 ms after stimulus onset (mean ±std across mice, Figure 3C) consistent with previous reports (Niell and Stryker, 2008).
evidence: This is measured from local field potential recordings shown in Figure 3C and consistent with prior work.

claim: The onset of cortical response was quantified as the earliest deflection in the local field potential that exceeded three standard deviations from baseline.
source: The onset of cortical response was quantified as the earliest deflection in the local field potential that exceeded three standard deviations from baseline.
evidence: This describes the method for determining cortical response onset.

claim: The earliest deflection in the local field potential corresponded to layer 4 of V1 based on current source density analysis.
source: We verified that the earliest deflection corresponded to layer 4 of V1, the major thalamo-recipient layer, based on current source density analysis (Niell and Stryker, 2008) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by current source density analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: About half of the neurons (46%) discriminated the target from the distractor when their activity was integrated over 300 ms.
source: About half of the neurons (46%) discriminated the target from the distractor when their activity was integrated over a time window of 300 ms, starting at the onset the cortical response and ending just before the stimulus could be moved by the animal (Figure 3E) (p<0.012, Wilcoxon ranksum test on spike counts across trials, Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons).
evidence: This is based on ROC analysis of single unit recordings shown in Figure 3E.

claim: At 40 ms after the onset of the cortical response only ~20% of discriminating units discriminated the target from the distractor above chance.
source: While at 40 ms after the onset of the cortical response only ~20% of the discriminating units discriminated the target from the distractor above chance, by 80 ms already ~50% of units did so with a median discrimination accuracy of 66% (range: 58–79%).
evidence: This is based on ROC analysis at different time intervals shown in Figure 3E-F.

claim: By 80 ms after cortical response onset, ~50% of discriminating units discriminated the target from the distractor with a median discrimination accuracy of 66%.
source: While at 40 ms after the onset of the cortical response only ~20% of the discriminating units discriminated the target from the distractor above chance, by 80 ms already ~50% of units did so with a median discrimination accuracy of 66% (range: 58–79%).
evidence: This is based on ROC analysis shown in Figure 3E-F.

claim: By 300 ms after cortical response onset, discriminating units reached a median discrimination accuracy of 74%.
source: The fraction of discriminating units discriminating increased more slowly following these initial 80 ms. By 300 ms (when, per definition, 100% of discriminating units are discriminating) they reached a median discrimination accuracy of 74% (range: 58–96%).
evidence: This is based on ROC analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Most discriminating units that preferred the target during the task showed a peak response to orientations larger than 90 degrees during passive viewing.
source: Most discriminating units that preferred the target during the task showed a peak response to orientations larger than 90 degrees (109 ± 8 degrees, median ±SEM; n = 9, four mice; Figure 3G).
evidence: This is based on orientation tuning measurements shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Most discriminating units that preferred the distractor during the task showed a peak response to orientations less than 45 degrees during passive viewing.
source: Furthermore most discriminating units that preferred the distractor during the task, showed a peak response to orientations less than 45 degrees (30 ± 20 degrees, median ±SEM; Figure 3G; n = 8, four mice).
evidence: This is based on orientation tuning measurements shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The difference in spike number during passive viewing correlated with how well discriminating units distinguish the target from the distractor during the task.
source: We compared the difference in spike number in response to grating presented at 45 and 90 degrees during passive viewing with how well discriminating units distinguish the target from the distractor during the task. The difference in spike number during passive viewing correlated with the value obtained from ROC analysis over the initial 80 ms following the onset of cortical response during the task (R2 based on linear fit: 0.35; Figure 3H).
evidence: This correlation is shown in Figure 3H.

claim: When cortical silencing followed the onset of cortical response by 44 ± 6 ms, the performance was close to chance (54 ± 5%).
source: When cortical silencing followed the onset of cortical response by 44 ± 6 ms the performance was close to chance (54 ± 5%; mean ±std across mice, Figure 4D), similar to when the LED onset preceded stimulus presentation (51 ± 3%; mean ±std across mice).
evidence: This is based on behavioral performance during optogenetic silencing shown in Figure 4D.

claim: When cortical silencing was delayed by 80 ms after the onset of the cortical response, performance accuracy increased to 76 ± 7%.
source: Strikingly, however, when cortical silencing was delayed by a further 40 ms, hence with a latency of 80 ms after the onset of the cortical response, performance accuracy of the animals sharply increased to 76 ± 7% (mean ±std across mice).
evidence: This is based on behavioral performance during optogenetic silencing shown in Figure 4D.

claim: When the LED onset followed the onset of the cortical response by 300 ms, animals performed similarly to control conditions (94 ± 2%).
source: Performance accuracy continued to increase, yet less sharply, over the longer intervals tested reaching 92 ± 5% when the LED onset followed the onset of the cortical response by 300 ms (mean ±std across mice). With this interval the animals performed similarly to control conditions, in the absence of LED illumination (94 ± 2%; mean ±std across mice).
evidence: This is based on behavioral performance during optogenetic silencing shown in Figure 4D.

claim: There is a sharp increase in performance when visual cortex is allowed to function between 44 and 80 ms after the onset of the cortical response.
source: Thus, there is a sharp increase in performance when visual cortex is allowed to function between 44 and 80 ms after the onset of the cortical response.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the behavioral data in Figure 4D.

claim: The minimal duration of visually evoked activity in V1 for an animal to perform the task above chance lies between 40 and 80 ms.
source: These results show that the minimal duration of visually evoked activity in V1 for an animal to perform the present task above chance lies between 40 and 80 ms.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the optogenetic silencing experiments in Figure 4.

claim: Performance accuracy in trials when V1 is active for only 80 ms is very sensitive to the difficulty of the task.
source: If the estimated time window indeed approximates the threshold duration of V1 activity for perceptual discrimination, performance accuracy in trials when V1 is active for only 80 ms should be very sensitive to the difficulty of the task.
evidence: This is a prediction tested in the harder discrimination task.

claim: Silencing cortex at 80 ms after the onset of the cortical response reduced performance significantly more for the 15 degrees discrimination task compared to the 45 degrees task.
source: Silencing cortex at 80 ms after the onset of the cortical response reduced performance significantly more for the 15 degrees as compared to the 45 degrees discrimination task in all animals (p<0.05, Wilcoxon ranksum test on choice data, n = 3 mice Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This is based on behavioral performance in the harder discrimination task shown in Figure 5B,C.

claim: Silencing V1 80 ms following the onset of the cortical response still enabled the 15 degrees discrimination to occur above chance.
source: While silencing V1 80 ms following the onset of the cortical response still enabled the 15 degrees discrimination to occur above chance (p<0.02, Wilcoxon ranksum test on choice data, n = 3 mice), the accuracy was significantly lower than for 45 degrees discrimination (p<0.02, Wilcoxon ranksum test on choice data, n = 3 mice, Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This is based on behavioral performance in the harder discrimination task shown in Figure 5B,C.

claim: The time between 40–80 ms following the onset of the cortical response captures the threshold duration of V1 activity for a simple perceptual discrimination.
source: Thus, these experiments demonstrate that the time between 40–80 ms following the onset of the cortical response indeed captures the threshold duration of V1 activity for a simple perceptual discrimination.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the harder discrimination task experiments in Figure 5.

claim: Over the initial 80 ms from the onset of the cortical response, discriminating units fired only 25 ± 4% of all the spikes fired above baseline during the 300 ms window.
source: Over these initial 80 ms from the onset of the cortical response discriminating units in primary visual cortex fired only 25 ± 4% of all the spikes fired above baseline during the 300 ms window (mean ±sem across units, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is based on analysis of spike counts shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: During the 80 ms interval, discriminating units fired 0.6 ± 0.1 action potentials in response to their preferred stimulus.
source: During this 80 ms interval discriminating units fired 0.6 ± 0.1 (median ±SEM across units) action potentials in response to their preferred stimulus (Figure 6F, response not different for the wild type and the transgenic mice as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), corresponding to a firing rate of 7.5 Hz, and 0.22 ± 0.06 action potentials for their non-preferred stimulus.
evidence: This is based on spike count analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: In response to their preferred stimulus, discriminating units fired only one or no action potential in 80% of the trials during the 80 ms interval.
source: Furthermore, in response to their preferred stimulus, discriminating units fired only one or no action potential in 80% of the trials and two action potentials in only 11% of the trials (Figure 6E), similar to what is expected by Poisson statistics (% of variance explained across units: R2 = 97 ± 5%, median ±SEM
evidence: This is based on spike count distributions shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The median time until first action potential was 70 ± 10 ms from the onset of the cortical response for the preferred stimulus.
source: median time until first action potential: 70 ± 10 ms and 80 ± 20 ms from the onset of the cortical response for the preferred and non-preferred stimulus, respectively (median ±SEM across units; analysis performed over the initial 300 ms from the onset of the cortical response, Figure 6C)
evidence: This is based on first spike timing analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The median time until first action potential was 80 ± 20 ms from the onset of the cortical response for the non-preferred stimulus.
source: median time until first action potential: 70 ± 10 ms and 80 ± 20 ms from the onset of the cortical response for the preferred and non-preferred stimulus, respectively (median ±SEM across units; analysis performed over the initial 300 ms from the onset of the cortical response, Figure 6C)
evidence: This is based on first spike timing analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The mean latency difference between first spikes for preferred and non-preferred stimuli was 12 ± 6 ms.
source: mean latency difference: 12 ± 6 ms (mean ±sem across units; p=0.03; t-test; Figure 6D)
evidence: This is based on first spike timing analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Over the initial 80 ms from the onset of the cortical response, the vast majority of discriminating units get to fire either one or no action potentials.
source: Thus, over the initial 80 ms from the onset of the cortical response the vast majority of discriminating units in primary visual cortex get to fire either one or no action potentials.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the spike count analysis in Figure 6.

claim: The first action potential was sufficient for ~33% of units to discriminate by 300 ms.
source: The first action potential was sufficient for ~33% of units to discriminate by 300 ms (compared to 46% if all the action potentials were available), and more than half of those units (54%) could discriminate above chance at 80 ms (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is based on ROC analysis using only first spikes shown in Figure 6G-H.

claim: For most units the first action potential substantially contributes to their ability to discriminate within the initial 80 ms after the onset of the cortical response.
source: Thus for most units the first action potential substantially contributes to their ability to discriminate within the initial 80 ms after the onset of the cortical response.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the first spike analysis in Figure 6G-H.

claim: The accuracy of the behavioral response during the initial 80 ms can be explained by pooling the activity of ~5 discriminating neurons on average.
source: Finally, the accuracy of the behavioral response during the initial 80 ms can be explained by pooling the activity of ~5 discriminating neurons on average (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), or ~20 neurons if non-discriminating neurons are also included in the pool (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is based on pooling analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The threshold duration of visually evoked cortical activity for a simple visual discrimination lies between 40 and 80 ms.
source: Taken together, these results show that the threshold duration of visually evoked cortical activity for a simple visual discrimination lies between 40 and 80 ms, a time window during which most individual cortical neurons get to fire one or no spike.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from all the experimental results.

claim: Both acute cortical silencing and permanent ablation reduce performance of the visual discrimination task to chance.
source: We have developed a visual discrimination task that necessitates visual cortex because both acute cortical silencing and permanent ablation reduces performance of the task to chance.
evidence: This summarizes the findings from Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The lower temporal limits of visually evoked activity for a perceptual discrimination lie within 40–80 ms.
source: By silencing visual cortex at various intervals following the onset of the cortical response we show that the lower temporal limits of visually evoked activity for a perceptual discrimination lie within 40–80 ms.
evidence: This summarizes the findings from Figure 4.

claim: The impact on behavioral performance when silencing visual cortex during the 40-80 ms time window is particularly sensitive to the difficulty of the task.
source: The impact on behavioral performance when silencing visual cortex during this time window is particularly sensitive to the difficulty of the task.
evidence: This summarizes the findings from Figure 5.

claim: During the initial 80 ms window, most neurons in primary visual cortex that disambiguate the identity of the stimulus fire either none or one action potential.
source: Importantly, during this initial 80 ms window, most of the neurons in primary visual cortex that disambiguate the identity of the stimulus fire either none or one action potential.
evidence: This summarizes the findings from Figure 6.

claim: The simple detection of a stimulus can be reported by an animal in response to direct cortical stimulation eliciting not more than one action potential in individual neurons.
source: The simple detection of a stimulus can be reported by an animal in response to direct cortical stimulation eliciting not more than one action potential in individual neurons (Histed and Maunsell, 2014).
evidence: This is cited from Histed and Maunsell, 2014.

claim: Stimulus discrimination via cortical stimulation has been reported only in response to repetitive stimulation eliciting series of action potentials.
source: Stimulus discrimination via cortical stimulation, on the other hand has been reported only in response to repetitive stimulation eliciting series of action potentials (Romo et al., 1998).
evidence: This is cited from Romo et al., 1998.

claim: Mice can discriminate visual stimuli even when most neurons in visual cortex are prevented from firing more than their first action potential.
source: We show that mice can discriminate visual stimuli even when most neurons in visual cortex are prevented from firing more than their first action potential.
evidence: This is a key finding of the study based on the combination of optogenetic and electrophysiology data.

claim: The first sensory evoked spikes of mouse visual cortical neurons are sufficient to drive downstream areas for a reliable execution of the task.
source: Thus, the first sensory evoked spikes of mouse visual cortical neurons are sufficient to drive downstream areas for a reliable execution of the task.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the main findings of the study.

claim: Cortical areas can instruct downstream targets with only a fraction of their neurons firing a single spike.
source: This highlights the ability of cortical areas to instruct downstream targets with only a fraction of their neurons firing a single spike.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the main findings.

claim: Similar findings about the essential role of the first spikes have been reported in the early olfactory system.
source: Similar findings about the essential role of the first spikes have been reported in the early olfactory system (Resulaj and Rinberg, 2015; Wilson et al., 2017).
evidence: This cites related findings from the olfactory system.

claim: Extending the time window beyond 80 ms increases the animal's behavioral performance.
source: However, our data also clearly show that extending this time window increases (i) the animal's behavioral performance, (ii) the ability of an ideal observer to disambiguate the stimulus based on the spiking of individual neurons, and (iii) the fraction of neurons that can be used to disambiguate.
evidence: This is based on the data in Figures 3, 4, and 6.

claim: Extending the time window beyond 80 ms increases the ability of an ideal observer to disambiguate the stimulus based on the spiking of individual neurons.
source: However, our data also clearly show that extending this time window increases (i) the animal's behavioral performance, (ii) the ability of an ideal observer to disambiguate the stimulus based on the spiking of individual neurons, and (iii) the fraction of neurons that can be used to disambiguate.
evidence: This is based on the ROC analysis in Figure 3.

claim: Extending the time window beyond 80 ms increases the fraction of neurons that can be used to disambiguate the stimulus.
source: However, our data also clearly show that extending this time window increases (i) the animal's behavioral performance, (ii) the ability of an ideal observer to disambiguate the stimulus based on the spiking of individual neurons, and (iii) the fraction of neurons that can be used to disambiguate.
evidence: This is based on the data in Figure 3F.

claim: Extending the time window gives more neurons the opportunity to fire their first spike.
source: Extending the time window not only gives more neurons the opportunity to fire their first spike (Figure 6C,D), but also enables second and third visually evoked spikes to contribute to the discriminability of the stimulus (compare Figure 6G with Figure 3E).
evidence: This is based on the first spike timing analysis in Figure 6C,D.

claim: Extending the time window enables second and third visually evoked spikes to contribute to the discriminability of the stimulus.
source: Extending the time window not only gives more neurons the opportunity to fire their first spike (Figure 6C,D), but also enables second and third visually evoked spikes to contribute to the discriminability of the stimulus (compare Figure 6G with Figure 3E).
evidence: This is based on comparing ROC analysis with all spikes (Figure 3E) versus only first spikes (Figure 6G).

claim: The extent of the 40-80 ms time window for sensory processing is consistent with observations in somatosensory cortex during cortical silencing in a detection task.
source: The extent of this time window for sensory processing is consistent with observations in somatosensory cortex performed during cortical silencing in a detection task (Sachidhanandam et al., 2013).
evidence: This cites related findings from somatosensory cortex.

claim: The ability for a neuron to disambiguate two stimuli with only one or no spike depends on how distinct the response of that neuron is for those stimuli and on the trial to trial variability of its responses.
source: The ability for a neuron to disambiguate two stimuli with only one or no spike depends on how distinct the response of that neuron is for those stimuli and on the trial to trial variability of its responses (Figure 3G,H).
evidence: This is based on the orientation tuning and correlation analysis in Figure 3G,H.

claim: Visual cortical neurons in mice have orientation tuning functions with relatively broad half widths at half max averaging 30–40 degrees.
source: In mice, visual cortical neurons have orientation tuning functions with relatively broad half widths at half max averaging 30–40 degrees.
evidence: This is a known property of mouse visual cortical neurons.

claim: As the difference in orientation between target and distractor stimuli becomes narrower, more spikes per neuron or more neurons spiking may be necessary to disambiguate the stimuli.
source: Given the large trial to trial variability of visually evoked responses in cortical neurons, one may expect that as the difference in orientation between the target and distractor stimuli become narrower, and the overlap in the responses of individual neurons to different stimuli increases, more spikes per neurons, or more neurons spiking may be necessary to disambiguate the stimuli.
evidence: This is a logical inference about task difficulty.

claim: Visual cortex may need longer than 80 ms for narrower orientation differences between stimuli.
source: As a consequence visual cortex may need longer than 80 ms.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the inference about task difficulty.

claim: Animals trained to perform equally well on 45 and 15 degrees difference discrimination tasks are significantly more impaired on the 15 degrees task when limiting V1 activity to 80 ms.
source: Consistent with this, our results show that animals trained to perform equally well on a 45 and 15 degrees difference discrimination task, are significantly more impaired on the 15 degrees discrimination task when limiting V1 activity to 80 ms.
evidence: This is based on the harder discrimination task data in Figure 5.

claim: An independent observer accumulating spikes from around 100 neurons preferring the same stimulus would reliably discriminate the target from the distractor within the initial 30 ms from the onset of the cortical response.
source: Our analysis shows that an independent observer accumulating spikes from around 100 neurons preferring the same stimulus would reliably discriminate the target from the distractor within the initial 30 ms from the onset of the cortical response (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on the pooling analysis in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The minimal time window that downstream areas necessitate to extract sufficient stimulus information is longer than the minimal time window necessitated by an independent observer.
source: Because mice discriminate at chance when visual cortex is only active for 40 ms, the minimal time window that downstream areas necessitate to extract sufficient stimulus information is longer than the minimal time window necessitated by an independent observer.
evidence: This is an inference comparing the behavioral results with the pooling analysis.

claim: Downstream areas may integrate spikes over longer periods than strictly necessary due to having to overcome noise or unrelated changes.
source: This suggests that downstream areas integrate spikes over longer periods than strictly necessary which may either be due to having to overcome noise (Mazurek and Shadlen, 2002; Shadlen and Newsome, 1998) or unrelated changes, or having to first reconfigure population activity before stimulus information can be integrated.
evidence: This is speculation about why downstream areas need more time, with citations to relevant work.

claim: Downstream areas may need to first reconfigure population activity before stimulus information can be integrated.
source: This suggests that downstream areas integrate spikes over longer periods than strictly necessary which may either be due to having to overcome noise (Mazurek and Shadlen, 2002; Shadlen and Newsome, 1998) or unrelated changes, or having to first reconfigure population activity before stimulus information can be integrated.
evidence: This is speculation about why downstream areas need more time.

claim: Investigating why downstream areas need more time will require future identification of downstream areas involved in the task and recordings of neural activity from these areas while visual cortex is silenced.
source: Investigating these possibilities will require future identification of downstream areas involved in the task and recordings of neural activity from these areas while visual cortex is silenced.
evidence: This describes future experiments needed to address open questions.

claim: Visual cortex is not necessary for all visually guided behaviors in rodents.
source: What is the role of visual cortex in perceptual discrimination? Visual cortex is not necessary for all visually guided behaviors in rodents.
evidence: This is a known fact about rodent visual behavior.

claim: Animals can still perform visually guided behavior even following the silencing or ablation of visual cortex, suggesting the involvement of subcortical areas.
source: Several experiment have demonstrated that animals can still perform visually guided behavior even following the silencing or ablation of visual cortex suggesting the involvement of subcortical areas (Glickfeld et al., 2013; Liang et al., 2015; Petruno et al., 2013; Prusky and Douglas, 2004).
evidence: This cites prior work showing subcortical visual processing.

claim: Behaviors that do not require visual cortex are either innate or, when learned, enable simple stimulus detection rather than discrimination tasks.
source: These behaviors however, are either innate or, when learned, enable simple stimulus detection rather than discrimination tasks.
evidence: This characterizes the types of behaviors that can occur without visual cortex.

claim: Subcortical visual areas may enable mice to place the stimulus in the center of the monitor while the cortex is silenced.
source: Some of these subcortical visual areas may indeed enable our mice to place the stimulus in the center of the monitor while the cortex is silenced, yet other strategies are also possible.
evidence: This is speculation about how mice perform the motor aspect of the task during cortical silencing.

claim: Some mice showed a bias in the fine positioning of the stimulus within the center of the monitor while the cortex was silenced compared to non-silenced trials.
source: At a finer scale, some of our mice showed a bias in the fine positioning of the stimulus within the center of the monitor while the cortex was silenced compared to the non-silenced trials (Figure 1F and Figure 4B).
evidence: This observation is noted in Figures 1F and 4B.

claim: Visual cortex is required to enable discrimination, consistent with recent work.
source: Although we show that visual cortex is required to enable discrimination, consistent with recent work (Jurjut et al., 2017; Poort et al., 2015), one may debate whether visual cortex plays an instructive role by providing information disambiguating the target from the distractor to downstream areas or simply a permissive role by regulating the overall excitability of those downstream areas (Otchy et al., 2015).
evidence: This cites recent work showing visual cortex is required for discrimination.

claim: Permanent ablation of V1 in trained animals reduces task performance to chance levels even ten days following the lesion.
source: We show that permanent ablation of V1 in trained animals reduces task performance to chance levels even ten days following the lesion.
evidence: This is based on the lesion data in Figure 2.

claim: Following permanent ablation of motor cortical areas, behavior is regained within a few days without further training.
source: While acute silencing of these motor cortical areas impairs behavior, following permanent ablation of these same areas behavior is regained within a few days without further training (Otchy et al., 2015).
evidence: This cites work on motor cortex showing recovery after lesions.

claim: Motor cortical areas are considered permissive rather than instructive for the execution of behavior.
source: As a consequence these motor areas are considered permissive rather than instructive for the execution of the behavior (Otchy et al., 2015).
evidence: This cites the interpretation of motor cortex lesion studies.

claim: The absence of recovery after V1 ablation is consistent with an instructive role of V1.
source: Instead, given the absence of recovery, our ablation results are consistent with an instructive role of V1.
evidence: This is an inference from the lesion data in Figure 2.

claim: The fact that the animal behaves at chance upon silencing cortex before stimulus presentation is evidence for an instructive role of visual cortex.
source: However, the fact that on the one hand the animal behaves at chance upon silencing cortex before the stimulus presentation, rather than being only partially impaired, and on the other hand that just 80 ms of activity are sufficient to almost completely recover the behavior is further evidence, in our opinion, for an instructive role of visual cortex.
evidence: This is an argument for the instructive role based on the optogenetic data.

claim: The sufficiency of a sensory cortical area to elicit a perceptual decision has been demonstrated for the somatosensory and taste systems.
source: The sufficiency of a sensory cortical area to elicit a perceptual decision has been demonstrated for the somatosensory (O'Connor et al., 2013; Romo et al., 1998) and taste (Peng et al., 2015) systems
evidence: This cites prior work on sufficiency of sensory cortex.

claim: Controlled perturbations of visual areas have been shown to affect decision in a predictable manner.
source: and controlled perturbations of visual areas has been shown to affect decision (Salzman et al., 1990) in a predictable manner.
evidence: This cites prior work on visual cortex perturbations.

claim: The ability to artificially recapitulate the pattern of cortical activity elicited by a visual stimulus through direct cortical activation will eventually provide a definite answer about the instructive role of visual cortex.
source: The ability to artificially recapitulate the pattern of cortical activity elicited by a visual stimulus through direct cortical activation will eventually provide a definite answer (Häusser and Smith, 2007).
evidence: This is speculation about future experiments with citation.

claim: It is not clear whether the findings may generalize to the phenomenon of visual masking.
source: It is not clear whether our findings may generalize to the phenomenon of visual masking in which a second stimulus presented shortly after the first may render the first stimulus less visible or invisible.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation in generalizing the findings.

claim: The neural mechanisms underlying visual masking are not well understood.
source: The neural mechanisms underlying visual masking, that is how added activity from two stimuli generates the perceptual illusion of masking, are not well understood (Breitmeyer, 2008; Macknik and Livingstone, 1998).
evidence: This cites work on visual masking.

claim: The current study addresses the minimal duration of activity in response to a single stimulus able to trigger a perceptual decision.
source: In the current study we address the simpler and more basic question of the minimal duration of activity in response to a single stimulus still able of triggering a perceptual decision.
evidence: This clarifies the scope of the current study.

claim: The optogenetic approach silences neuronal activity while visual masking adds activity.
source: Indeed there are clear differences between visual masking and the optogenetic approach used here: First, our approach silences neuronal activity while visual masking adds activity (Macknik and Livingstone, 1998).
evidence: This contrasts the current approach with visual masking.

claim: The optogenetic approach is area specific while visual masking impacts the whole visual system.
source: Second, our approach is area specific while visual masking impacts the whole visual system.
evidence: This contrasts the current approach with visual masking.

claim: The optogenetic approach can silence visual cortex after most neurons have fired one or no spikes in response to the visual stimulus.
source: Finally, we can silence visual cortex after most neurons have fired one or no spikes in response to the visual stimulus while, during visual masking experiments, even the just perceivable stimuli elicit multiple spikes (Kovács et al., 1995; Lamme et al., 2002; Rolls et al., 1999).
evidence: This contrasts the current approach with visual masking, with citations.

claim: Future experiments using optogenetic approaches may help understand the neuronal mechanisms underlying the perceptual illusion of visual masking.
source: Future experiments using optogenetic approaches may help us understand the neuronal mechanisms underlying the perceptual illusion of visual masking.
evidence: This is speculation about future experiments.

claim: The study provides direct evidence for the minimal amount of time that it takes visual cortex to process visual information in order to enable a perceptual decision.
source: We have provided direct evidence for the minimal amount of time that it takes visual cortex to process visual information in order to enable a perceptual decision and determined the neuronal activity that occurs during that period.
evidence: This summarizes the main contribution of the study.

claim: The speed at which humans are able to discriminate visual stimuli has led to the suggestion that processing can be accomplished with individual neurons in each relevant brain area firing either none or one action potential.
source: The speed at which humans are able to discriminate visual stimuli has led to the suggestion that processing of the visual stimuli can be accomplished with individual neurons in each of the relevant brain areas firing either none or one action potential.
evidence: This references a hypothesis about rapid visual processing in humans.

claim: A period of activity in mouse primary visual cortex during which most neurons fire none or one action potential is sufficient to enable perceptual discrimination.
source: This work demonstrates that a period of activity in mouse primary visual cortex during which most neurons fire none or one action potential is indeed sufficient to enable perceptual discrimination.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Future work will elucidate which downstream brain areas read out the first essential spikes generated in V1.
source: Future work will elucidate which downstream brain areas read out these first essential spikes generated in V1.
evidence: This describes future directions for research.
